summary:
Russia prohibits legal gender recognition outright. The law signed by President Vladimir Putin in 2023 bans gender reassignment surgery and any change of gender marker on official documents, voids a marriage concluded by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex, and removes the right to adopt from people diagnosed with gender dysphoria.

For many transgender Russians emigration has become the only remaining means of living openly. Reporting published in June 2024 profiles people caught in limbo between leaving and staying, and analysis from August 2024 describes the court-driven purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians.

Public expression is constrained by the propaganda statutes. The 2013 law targeted material concerning minors; it was expanded in December 2022 to cover all age groups and now reaches content that promotes "non-traditional" sexual relationships, makes minors interested in gender transition, or gives minors a "desire to change their sex". The provisions reach speech that justifies gender transition.

Enforcement has grown sharply. More than 180 cases were brought under the propaganda provisions in 2023 alone, exceeding the total for 2013 to 2022 combined and producing roughly 26 million rubles in fines. Cases under these statutes have increased eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines brought over 60 million rubles (about $765,300) into the state budget in the two years to mid-2025.

Since the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of a non-existent "international LGBT movement" as extremist, charges have been brought for displaying the rainbow flag or its colours. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in that movement or display of its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, with charges drawn from both the administrative and criminal codes. Between March and May 2026, nine LGBTQ organisations, among them the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed as extremist.

The post-designation crackdown was immediate. Within 48 hours of the ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly bars in Moscow; about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night. Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ life through 2025. In December 2024 a man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Coercive conversion practice against trans people is documented. A transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a centre near Novosibirsk and held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour, escaping only after police responded to a phone she had found.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, does not designate hate crimes as such, and does not treat gender-identity or sexual-orientation motivation as an aggravating factor in sentencing. The state does not officially record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community.

Entry and onward-protection context carries an explicit warning for LGBT travellers. The US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes language relevant to LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

A 2024 law additionally bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that permit gender transitions, a rule that bears on foreign visitors in the country.
tangentialFactors:
No recognition of same-sex relationships exists: neither same-sex marriage nor civil unions are permitted, and same-sex couples are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex couples. In July 2020 voters approved a constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in Fedotova and Others v. Russia (2021) that Russia's refusal to offer any legal recognition to same-sex relationships violated human rights; Russia left that court in 2022. The same court fined Russia in 2010 for systematically refusing permits for pride parades, and Moscow authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally.

Public opinion provides the social backdrop to enforcement. A 2022 survey found 74% of Russians said homosexuality should not be accepted by society, up from 60% in 2002, and a September 2021 survey put support for equal rights for gays and lesbians at 33%.

Reporting on the scale of the fallout is consistent across outlets: an independent outlet described arrests, club raids and extremism charges as the defining features of LGBTQ life in 2025, and commentary from August 2024 characterised the court decision as driving the community into exile.
localsOnly:
Residents diagnosed with gender dysphoria lose the right to adopt children under the 2023 legislation, and any marriage entered into by a trans person with someone of their same birth sex is void. Gender reassignment surgery and any change of sex marker on state documents are barred, so domestic legal transition is unavailable regardless of medical diagnosis.

Resident organisations face dissolution as extremist organisations: nine LGBTQ groups, including the Russian LGBT Network, Coming Out and Centre T, were outlawed between March and May 2026. Display of rainbow symbols has drawn extremism-related charges since the November 2023 Supreme Court designation, and the state does not record hate crimes against the LGBTQ community, leaving victims without an official recognition of motive in sentencing.

Fines under the propaganda statutes fund the state: roughly 26 million rubles were imposed in 2023, and over 60 million rubles accrued to the budget across the two years to mid-2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 101 extremism-related convictions reported by Human Rights Watch in June 2025 cover participation in or display of symbols of the designated LGBT movement; the inventory does not separate how many of those charges concerned transgender people specifically, and no trans-specific conviction count is sourced.

Whether any administrative or clinical framework exists for trans people to obtain cross-sex hormone therapy without surgery, other than the documented coerced administration at a conversion centre near Novosibirsk, is not addressed by the inventory.

The enforcement figures for the propaganda statutes come from two sources using different windows (2023 alone, and the two years to mid-2025); the sources do not state whether the 2023 case total is counted under the pre-2022 or post-2022 version of the provisions.

The precise commencement date and implementing procedure of the 2024 ban on adoption by citizens or permanent residents of countries allowing gender transitions is unresolved in the inventory, as is whether the US Level 4 advisory's LGBT-specific wording has been revised since the advisory was last checked.

Conditions in the autonomous republic of Chechnya are referenced only through the UK Home Office asylum standard; no independent reporting on current enforcement there appears in the inventory.
